entries.a1b59962b6001f5f04aadb29646c0d33d63c8dc6: <div sID="gen10780" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="Ps.25" sID="Ps.25"/> <div eID="gen10780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10781" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10782" type="x-p"/> This psalm is full of devout affection to God, the out-goings of holy desires towards his favour and grace and the lively actings of faith in his promises. We may learn out of it, I. What it is to pray, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">15</reference>. II. What we must pray for, the pardon of sin (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.6-Ps.25.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.18">18</reference>), direction in the way of duty (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.4-Ps.25.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>), the favour of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.16">ver. 16</reference>), deliverance out of our troubles (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.17-Ps.25.18">ver. 17, 18</reference>), preservation from our enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.20-Ps.25.21">ver. 20, 21</reference>), and the salvation of the church of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.22">ver. 22</reference>. III. What we may plead in prayer, our confidence in God (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.2-Ps.25.3 Ps.25.5 Ps.25.20 Ps.25.21">ver. 2, 3, 5, 20, 21</reference>), our distress and the malice of our enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.17">ver. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.19">19</reference>), our sincerity, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.21">ver. 21</reference>. IV. What precious promises we have to encourage us in prayer, of guidance and instruction (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.8-Ps.25.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.12">12</reference>), the benefit of the covenant (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.10">ver. 10</reference>), and the pleasure of communion with God, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.13-Ps.25.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. It is easy to apply the several passages of this psalm to ourselves in the singing of it; for we have often troubles, and always sins, to complain of at the throne of grace.
entries.3d3c78da2a1a7a0bf1c2ee5c03fc1297296ebc21: <div eID="gen10782" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10781" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Earnest Supplications.</title> <div sID="gen10783" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , do I lift up my soul. <hi type="super">2</hi> O my God, I trust in thee: let me not be ashamed, let not mine enemies triumph over me. 3 Yea, let none that wait on thee be ashamed: let them be ashamed which transgress without cause. <hi type="super">4</hi> show me thy ways, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; teach me thy paths. <hi type="super">5</hi> Lead me in thy truth, and teach me: for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the God of my salvation; on thee do I wait all the day. <hi type="super">6</hi> Remember, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , thy tender mercies and thy lovingkindnesses; for they <hi type="italic">have been</hi> ever of old. <hi type="super">7</hi> Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me for thy goodness' sake, O <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen10783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10784" type="x-p"/> Here we have David's professions of desire towards God and dependence on him. He often begins his psalms with such professions, not to move God, but to move himself, and to engage himself to answer those professions. <div eID="gen10784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10785" type="x-p"/> I. He professes his desire towards God: <hi type="italic">Unto thee, O Lord! do I lift up my soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">v. 1</reference>. In the foregoing psalm (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">v. 4</reference>) it was made the character of a good man that he <hi type="italic">has not lifted up his soul to vanity;</hi> and a call was given to the everlasting gates to lift up their heads for the <hi type="italic">King of glory to come in,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">v. 1</reference>. To this character, to this call, David here answers, "Lord, I lift up my soul, not to vanity, but to thee." Note, In worshipping God we must lift up our souls to him. Prayer is the ascent of the soul to God; God must be eyed and the soul employed. <hi type="italic">Sursum corda—Up with you hearts,</hi> was anciently used as a call to devotion. With a holy contempt of the world and the things of it, by a fixed thought and active faith, we must set God before us, and let out our desires towards him as the fountain of our happiness. <div eID="gen10785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10786" type="x-p"/> II. He professes his dependence upon God and begs for the benefit and comfort of that dependence (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">O my God! I trust in thee.</hi> His conscience witnessed for him that he had no confidence in himself nor in any creature, and that he had no diffidence of God or of his power or promise. He pleases himself with this profession of faith in God. Having put his trust in God, he is easy, is well satisfied, and quiet from the fear of evil; and he pleads it with God whose honour it is to help those that honour him by trusting in him. What men put a confidence in is either their joy or their shame, according as it proves. Now David here, under the direction of faith, prays earnestly, 1. That shame might not be his lot: "<hi type="italic">Let me not be ashamed</hi> of my confidence in thee; let me not be shaken from it by any prevailing fears, and let me not be, in the issue, disappointed of what I depend upon thee for; but, Lord, <hi type="italic">keep what I have committed unto thee.</hi>" Note, If we make our confidence in God our stay, it shall not be our shame; and, if we triumph in him, our enemies shall not triumph over us, as they would if we should now sink under our fears, or should, in the issue, come short of our hopes. 2. That it might not be the lot of any that trusted in God. All the saints have obtained a like precious faith; and therefore, doubtless, it will be alike successful in the issue. Thus the communion of saints is kept up, even by their praying one for another. True saints will make supplication for all saints. It is certain that none who, by a believing attendance, wait on God, and, by a believing hope, wait for him, shall be made ashamed of it. 3. That it might be the lot of the transgressors; <hi type="italic">Let those be ashamed that transgress without cause,</hi> or <hi type="italic">vainly,</hi> as the word is. (1.) Upon no provocation. They revolt from God and their duty, from David and his government (so some), without any occasion given them, not being able to pretend any iniquity they have found in God, or that in any thing he has wearied them. The weaker the temptation is by which men are drawn to sin the stronger the corruption is by which they are driven by it. Those are the worst transgressors that sin for sinning-sake. (2.) To no purpose. They know their attempts against God are fruitless; they imagine a vain thing, and therefore they will soon be ashamed of it. <div eID="gen10786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10787" type="x-p"/> III. He begs direction from God in the way of his duty, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.4-Ps.25.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. Once and again he here prays to God to teach him. He was a knowing man himself, but the most intelligent, the most observant, both need and desire to be taught of God; from him we must be ever learning. Observe, <div eID="gen10787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10788" type="x-p"/> 1. What he desired to learn: "<hi type="italic">Teach me,</hi> not fine words or fine notions, but <hi type="italic">thy ways, thy paths, thy truth,</hi> the ways in which thou walkest towards men, which are <hi type="italic">all mercy and truth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.10">v. 10</reference>), and the ways in which thou wouldst have me to walk towards thee." Those are best taught who understand their duty, and know <hi type="italic">the good things they should do,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.3">Eccl. ii. 3</reference>. God's <hi type="italic">paths</hi> and his <hi type="italic">truth</hi> are the same; divine laws are all founded upon divine truths. The way of God's precepts is the way of truth, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.30">Ps. cxix. 30</reference>. Christ is both the way and the truth, and therefore we must learn Christ. <div eID="gen10788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10789" type="x-p"/> 2. What he desired of God, in order to this. (1.) That he would enlighten his understanding concerning his duty: "<hi type="italic">Show me thy way,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">teach me.</hi>" In doubtful cases we should pray earnestly that God would make it plain to us what he would have us to do. (2.) That he would incline his will to do it, and strengthen him in it: "<hi type="italic">Lead me,</hi> and so teach me." Not only as we lead one that is dimsighted, to keep him from missing his way, but as we lead one that is sick, and feeble, and faint, to help him forward in the way and to keep him from fainting and falling. We go no further in the way to heaven than God is pleased to lead us and to hold us up. <div eID="gen10789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10790" type="x-p"/> 3. What he pleads, (1.) His great expectation from God: <hi type="italic">Thou art the God of my salvation.</hi> Note, Those that choose salvation of God as their end, and make him the God of their salvation, may come boldly to him for direction in the way that leads to that end. If God save us, he will teach us and lead us. He that gives salvation will give instruction. (2.) His constant attendance on God: <hi type="italic">On thee do I wait all the day.</hi> Whence should a servant expect direction what to do but from his own master, on whom he waits all the day? If we sincerely desire to know our duty, with a resolution to do it, we need not question but that God will direct us in it. <div eID="gen10790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10791" type="x-p"/> IV. He appeals to God's infinite mercy, and casts himself upon that, not pretending to any merit of his own (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Remember, O Lord! thy tender mercies,</hi> and, for the sake of those mercies, lead me, and teach me; for they <hi type="italic">have been ever of old.</hi>" 1. "Thou always wast a merciful God; it is thy name, it is thy nature and property, to show mercy." 2. "Thy counsels and designs of mercy were from everlasting; the vessels of mercy were, before all worlds, ordained to glory." 3. "The instances of thy mercy to the church in general, and to me in particular, were early and ancient, and constant hitherto; they began of old, and never ceased. Thou hast taught me from my youth up, teach me now." <div eID="gen10791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10792" type="x-p"/> V. He is in a special manner earnest for the pardon of his sins (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O remember not the sins of my youth.</hi> Lord, remember thy mercies (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.6">v. 6</reference>), which speak for me, and not my sins, which speak against me." Here is, 1. An implicit confession of sin; he specifies particularly the sins of his youth. Note, Our youthful faults and follies should be matter of our repentance and humiliation long after, because time does not wear out the guilt of sin. Old people should mourn for the sinful mirth and be in pain for the sinful pleasures of their youth. He aggravates his sins, calling them his <hi type="italic">transgressions;</hi> and the more holy, just, and good the law is, which sin is the transgression of, the more exceedingly sinful it ought to appear to us. 2. An express petition for mercy, (1.) That he might be acquitted from guilt: "<hi type="italic">Remember not the sins of my youth;</hi> that is, remember them not against me, lay them not to my charge, enter not into judgment with me for them." When God pardons sin he is said to <hi type="italic">remember it no more,</hi> which denotes a plenary remission; he forgives and forgets. (2.) That he might be accepted in God's sight: "Remember thou me; think on me for good, and come in seasonably for my succour." We need desire no more to make us happy than for God to remember us with favour. His plea is, "according to thy mercy, and for thy goodness-sake." Note, It is God's goodness and not ours, his mercy and not our own merit, that must be our plea for the pardon of sin and all the good we stand in need of. This plea we must always rely upon, as those that are sensible of our poverty and unworthiness and as those that are satisfied of the riches of God's mercy and grace.
entries.83adde49cbfb500757b78b35224a67dcad855df2: <div eID="gen10792" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Divine Goodness and Mercy.</title> <div sID="gen10793" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Good and upright <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : therefore will he teach sinners in the way. <hi type="super">9</hi> The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way. <hi type="super">10</hi> All the paths of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">are</hi> mercy and truth unto such as keep his covenant and his testimonies. <hi type="super">11</hi> For thy name's sake, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , pardon mine iniquity; for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> great. <hi type="super">12</hi> What man <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that feareth the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? him shall he teach in the way <hi type="italic">that</hi> he shall choose. <hi type="super">13</hi> His soul shall dwell at ease; and his seed shall inherit the earth. <hi type="super">14</hi> The secret of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> with them that fear him; and he will show them his covenant. <div eID="gen10793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10794" type="x-p"/> God's promises are here mixed with David's prayers. Many petitions there were in the former part of the psalm, and many we shall find in the latter; and here, in the middle of the psalm, he meditates upon the promises, and by a lively faith sucks and is satisfied from these breasts of consolation; for the promises of God are not only the best foundation of prayer, telling us what to pray for and encouraging our faith and hope in prayer, but they are a present answer to prayer. Let the prayer be made according to the promise, and then the promise may be read as a return to the prayer; and we are to believe the prayer is heard because the promise will be performed. But, in the midst of the promises, we fine one petition which seems to come in somewhat abruptly, and should have followed upon <reference osisRef="Ps.25.7">v. 7</reference>. It is that (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Pardon my iniquity.</hi> But prayers for the pardon of sin are never impertinent; we mingle sin with all our actions, and therefore should mingle such prayers with all our devotions. He enforces this petition with a double plea. The former is very natural: "<hi type="italic">For thy name's sake pardon my iniquity,</hi> because thou hast proclaimed thy name gracious and merciful, pardoning iniquity, for thy glory-sake, for thy promise-sake, for thy own sake," <reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Isa. xliii. 25</reference>. But the latter is very surprising: "<hi type="italic">Pardon my iniquity, for it is great,</hi> and the greater it is the more will divine mercy be magnified in the forgiveness of it." It is the glory of a great God to forgive great sins, to forgive iniquity, transgression, and sin, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.7">Exod. xxxiv. 7</reference>. "It is great, and therefore I am undone, for ever undone, if infinite mercy do not interpose for the pardon of it. It is great; I see it to be so." The more we see of the heinousness of our sins the better qualified we are to find mercy with God. When we confess sin we must aggravate it. <div eID="gen10794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10795" type="x-p"/> Let us now take a view of the great and precious promises which we have in these verses, and observe, <div eID="gen10795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10796" type="x-p"/> I. To whom these promises belong and who may expect the benefit of them. We are all sinners; and can we hope for any advantage by them? Yes (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.8">v. 8</reference>), He will teach sinners, though they be sinners; for Christ came into the world to save sinners, and, in order to that, to teach sinners, to call sinners to repentance. These promises are sure to those who though they have been sinners, have gone astray, yet now keep God's word, 1. To such as keep his covenant and his testimonies (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.10">v. 10</reference>), such as take his precepts for their rule and his promises for their portion, such as, having taken God to be to them a God, live upon that, and, having given up themselves to be him a people, live up to that. Though, through the infirmity of the flesh, they sometimes break the command, yet by a sincere repentance when at any time they do amiss, and a constant adherence by faith to God as their God, they keep the covenant and do not break that. 2. To such as fear him (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.12">v. 12</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">v. 14</reference>), such as stand in awe of his majesty and worship him with reverence, submit to his authority and obey him with cheerfulness, dread his wrath and are afraid of offending him. <div eID="gen10796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10797" type="x-p"/> II. Upon what these promises are grounded, and what encouragement we have to build upon them. Here are two things which ratify and confirm all the promises:—1. The perfections of God's nature. We value the promise by the character of him that makes its. We may therefore depend upon God's promises; for <hi type="italic">good and upright is the Lord,</hi> and therefore he will be as good as his word. He is so kind that he cannot deceive us, so true that he cannot break his promise. <hi type="italic">Faithful is he who hath promised,</hi> who also will do it. He was good in making the promise, and therefore will be upright in performing it. 2. The agreeableness of all he says and does with the perfections of his nature (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">All the paths of the Lord</hi> (that is, all his promises and all his providences) <hi type="italic">are mercy and truth;</hi> they are, like himself, good and upright. All God's dealings with his people are according to the mercy of his purposes and the truth of his promises; all he does comes from love, covenant-love; and they may see in it his mercy displayed and his word fulfilled. What a rich satisfaction may this be to good people, that, whatever afflictions they are exercised with, <hi type="italic">All the paths of the Lord are mercy and truth,</hi> and so it will appear when they come to their journey's end. <div eID="gen10797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10798" type="x-p"/> III. What these promises are. <div eID="gen10798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10799" type="x-p"/> 1. That God will instruct and direct them in the way of their duty. This is most insisted upon, because it is an answer to David's prayers (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.4-Ps.25.5">v. 4, 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Show me thy ways and lead me.</hi> We should fix our thoughts, and act our faith, most on those promises which suit our present case. (1.) He will <hi type="italic">teach sinners in the way,</hi> because they are sinners, and therefore need teaching. When they see themselves sinners, and desire teaching, then he will teach them the way of reconciliation to God, the way to a well-grounded peace of conscience, and the way to eternal life. He does, by his gospel, make this way known to all, and, by his Spirit, open the understanding and guide penitent sinners that enquire after it. The devil leads men blindfold to hell, but God enlightens men's eyes, sets things before them in a true light, and so leads them to heaven. (2.) <hi type="italic">The meek will he guide,</hi> the meek will he teach, that is, those that are humble and low in their own eyes, that are distrustful of themselves, desirous to be taught, and honestly resolved to follow the divine guidance. <hi type="italic">Speak, Lord, for thy servant hears.</hi> These he will guide <hi type="italic">in judgment,</hi> that is, by the rule of the written word; he will guide them in that which is practical, which relates to sin and duty, so that they may keep conscience void of offence; and he will do it judiciously (so some), that is, he will suit his conduct to their case; he will teach sinners with wisdom, tenderness, and compassion, and as they are able to bear. He will teach them his way. All good people make God's way their way, and desire to be taught that; and those that do so shall be taught and led in that way. (3.) <hi type="italic">Him that feareth the Lord he will teach in the way that he shall choose,</hi> either in the way that God shall choose or that the good man shall choose. It comes all to one, for he that fears the Lord chooses the things that please him. If we choose the right way, he that directed our choice will direct our steps, and will lead us in it. If we choose wisely, God will give us grace to walk wisely. <div eID="gen10799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10800" type="x-p"/> 2. That God will make them easy (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">His soul shall dwell at ease, shall lodge in goodness,</hi> marg. Those that devote themselves to the fear of God, and give themselves to be taught of God, will be easy, if it be not their own fault. The soul that is sanctified by the grace of God, and, much more, that is comforted by the peace of God, dwells at ease. Even when the body is sick and lies in pain, yet the soul may dwell at ease in God, may return to him, and repose in him as its rest. Many things occur to make us uneasy, but there is enough in the covenant of grace to counterbalance them all and to make us easy. <div eID="gen10800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10801" type="x-p"/> 3. That he will give to them and theirs as much of this world as is good for them: <hi type="italic">His seed shall inherit the earth.</hi> Next to our care concerning our souls is our care concerning our seed, and God has a blessing in store for the generation of the upright. Those that fear God shall inherit the earth, shall have a competency in it and the comfort of it, and their children shall fare the better for their prayers when they are gone. <div eID="gen10801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10802" type="x-p"/> 4. That God will admit them into the secret of communion with himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">The secret of the Lord is with those that fear him.</hi> They understand his word; for, <hi type="italic">if any man do his will, he shall know of the doctrine whether it be of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. Those that receive the truth in the love of it, and experience the power of it, best understand the mystery of it. They know the meaning of his providence, and what God is doing with them, better than others. <hi type="italic">Shall I hide from Abraham the things that I do?</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.18.17">Gen. xviii. 17</reference>. He call them not <hi type="italic">servants,</hi> but <hi type="italic">friends,</hi> as he called Abraham. They know by experience the blessings of the covenant and the pleasure of that fellowship which gracious souls have with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. This honour have all his saints.
entries.ddc47d828c082a8d86de239b7cfadd47dd0fb4a5: <div eID="gen10802" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Precious Promises; Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen10803" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Mine eyes <hi type="italic">are</hi> ever toward the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net. <hi type="super">16</hi> Turn thee unto me, and have mercy upon me; for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> desolate and afflicted. <hi type="super">17</hi> The troubles of my heart are enlarged: <hi type="italic">O</hi> bring thou me out of my distresses. 18 Look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins. <hi type="super">19</hi> Consider mine enemies; for they are many; and they hate me with cruel hatred. <hi type="super">20</hi> O keep my soul, and deliver me: let me not be ashamed; for I put my trust in thee. <hi type="super">21</hi> Let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on thee. 22 Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles. <div eID="gen10803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10804" type="x-p"/> David, encouraged by the promises he had been meditating upon, here renews his addresses to God, and concludes the psalm, as he began, with professions of dependence upon God and desire towards him. <div eID="gen10804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10805" type="x-p"/> I. He lays open before God the calamitous condition he was in. His feet were in the net, held fast and entangled, so that he could not extricate himself out of his difficulties, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">v. 15</reference>. He was <hi type="italic">desolate and afflicted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.16">v. 16</reference>. It is common for those that are afflicted to be desolate; their friends desert them then, and they are themselves disposed to sit alone and keep silence, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.28">Lam. iii. 28</reference>. David calls himself <hi type="italic">desolate and solitary</hi> because he depended not upon his servants and soldiers, but relied as entirely upon God as if he had no prospect at all of help and succour from any creature. Being in distress, in many distresses, <hi type="italic">the troubles of his heart were enlarged</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.17">v. 17</reference>), he grew more and more melancholy and troubled in mind. Sense of sin afflicted him more than any thing else: this it was that broke and wounded his spirit, and made his outward troubles lie heavily upon him. He was in <hi type="italic">affliction and pain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.18">v. 18</reference>. His enemies that persecuted him were many and malicious (they hated him), and very barbarous; it was <hi type="italic">with a cruel hatred</hi> that they hated him, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.19">v. 19</reference>. Such were Christ's enemies and the persecutors of his church. <div eID="gen10805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10806" type="x-p"/> II. He expresses the dependence he had upon God in these distresses (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">My eyes are ever towards the Lord.</hi> Idolaters were for gods that they could see with their bodily eyes, and they had their eyes ever towards their idols, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.7-Isa.17.8">Isa. xvii. 7, 8</reference>. But it is an eye of faith that we must have towards God, who is a Spirit, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.1">Zech. ix. 1</reference>. Our meditation of him must be sweet, and we must always set him before us: in all our ways we must acknowledge him and do all to his glory. Thus we must live a life of communion with God, not only in ordinances, but in providences, not only in acts of devotion, but in the whole course of our conversation. David had the comfort of this in his affliction; for, because his eyes were ever towards the Lord, he doubted not but he would pluck his feet out of the net, that he would deliver him from the corruptions of his own heart (so some), from the designs of his enemies against him, so others. Those that have their eye ever towards God shall not have their feet long in the net. He repeats his profession of dependence upon God (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.20">v. 20</reference>)—<hi type="italic">Let me not be ashamed, for I put my trust in thee;</hi> and of expectation from him—<hi type="italic">I wait on thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.21">v. 21</reference>. It is good thus to hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord. <div eID="gen10806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10807" type="x-p"/> III. He prays earnestly to God for relief and succour, <div eID="gen10807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10808" type="x-p"/> 1. For himself. <div eID="gen10808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10809" type="x-p"/> (1.) See how he begs, [1.] For the remission of sin (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Forgive all my sins.</hi> Those were his heaviest burdens, and which brought upon him all other burdens. He had begged (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.7">v. 7</reference>) for the pardon of the sins of his youth, and (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.11">v. 11</reference>) for the pardon of some one particular iniquity that was remarkably great, which some think, was his sin in the matter of Uriah. But here he prays, Lord, <hi type="italic">forgive all, take away all iniquity.</hi> It is observable that, as to his affliction, he asks for no more than God's regard to it: "<hi type="italic">Look upon my affliction and my pain,</hi> and do with it as thou pleasest." But, as to his sin, he asks for no less than a full pardon: <hi type="italic">Forgive all my sins.</hi> When at any time we are in trouble we should be more concerned about our sins, to get them pardoned, than about our afflictions, to get them removed. Yet he prays, [2.] For the redress of his grievances. His mind was troubled for God's withdrawings from him and under the sense he had of his displeasure against him for his sins; and therefore he prays (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.16">v. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">Turn thou unto me.</hi> And, if God turn to us, no matter who turns from us. His condition was troubled, and, in reference to that, he prays, "<hi type="italic">O bring thou me out of my distresses.</hi> I see no way of deliverance open; but thou canst either find one or make one." His enemies were spiteful; and in reference to that, he prays, "<hi type="italic">O keep my soul</hi> from falling into their hands, or else <hi type="italic">deliver me</hi> out of their hands." <div eID="gen10809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10810" type="x-p"/> (2.) Four things he mentions by way of plea to enforce these petitions, and refers himself and them to God's consideration:—[1.] He pleads God's mercy: <hi type="italic">Have mercy upon me.</hi> Men of the greatest merits would be undone if they had not to do with a God of infinite mercies. [2.] He pleads his own misery, the distress he was in, his affliction and pain, especially the troubles of his heart, all which made him the proper object of divine mercy. [3.] He pleads the iniquity of his enemies: "Lord, consider them, how cruel they are, and deliver me out of their hands." [4.] He pleads his own integrity, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.12">v. 12</reference>. Though he had owned himself guilty before God, and had confessed his sins against him, yet, as to his enemies, he had the testimony of his conscience that he had done them no wrong, which was his comfort when they hated him with cruel hatred; and he prays that this might <hi type="italic">preserve him,</hi> This intimates that he did not expect to be safe any longer than he continued in his <hi type="italic">integrity and uprightness,</hi> and that, while he did continue in it, he did not doubt of being safe. Sincerity will be our best security in the worst of times. Integrity and uprightness will be a man's preservation more than the wealth and honour of the world can be. These will preserve us to the heavenly kingdom. We should therefore pray to God to preserve us in our integrity and then be assured that that will preserve us. <div eID="gen10810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10811" type="x-p"/> 2. For the church of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Redeem Israel, O God! out of all his troubles.</hi> David was now in trouble himself, but he thinks it not strange, since trouble is the lot of all God's Israel. Why should any one member fare better than the whole body? David's troubles were enlarged, and very earnest he was with God to deliver him, yet he forgets not the distresses of God's church; for, when we have ever so much business of our own at the throne of grace, we must still remember to pray for the public. Good men have little comfort in their own safety while the church is in distress and danger. This prayer is a prophecy that God would, at length, give David rest, and therewith give Israel rest from all their enemies round about. It is a prophecy of the sending of the Messiah in due time to <hi type="italic">redeem Israel from his iniquities</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.8">Ps. cxxx. 8</reference>) and so to redeem them from their troubles. It refers also to the happiness of the future state. In heaven, and in heaven only, will God's Israel be perfectly redeemed from all troubles.  <chapter eID="Ps.25"/> <div eID="gen10811" type="x-p"/>

entries.2a0d2b5f47a5e36b95e57aeda7305c019750c1c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5714"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 25</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.25.1-Ps.25.22">Psa 25:1-22</reference>. The general tone of this Psalm is that of prayer for help from enemies. Distress, however, exciting a sense of sin, humble confession, supplication for pardon, preservation from sin, and divine guidance, are prominent topics.</title> <div sID="gen8698" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5714"/><hi type="bold">1. lift up my soul--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">Psa 24:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.4">86:4</reference>), set my affections (compare <reference osisRef="Col.3.2">Col 3:2</reference>). <div eID="gen8698" type="x-p"/>
entries.3084c10137abcba8bbe1a31db7adce9a0355e218: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5715"/><div sID="gen8699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5715"/><hi type="bold">2. not be ashamed--</hi>by disappointment of hopes of relief. <div eID="gen8699" type="x-p"/>
entries.3750ba287f84b963ea1da498591fc3ae43428f58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5716"/><div sID="gen8700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5716"/><hi type="bold">3. The prayer generalized as to all who wait on God--</hi>that is, who expect His favor. On the other hand, the disappointment of the perfidious, who, unprovoked, have done evil, is invoked (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.9">2Sa 22:9</reference>). <div eID="gen8700" type="x-p"/>
entries.aab7e92ec793f862b6cef129a84bcbaf54d42674: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5717"/><div sID="gen8701" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5717"/>4-5. On the ground of former favor, he invokes divine guidance, according to God's gracious ways of dealing and faithfulness. <div eID="gen8701" type="x-p"/>
entries.3224a4ac42aa2d62701b1063d3a29c5d29d6fcfe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5718"/><div sID="gen8702" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5718"/>6-7. Confessing past and present sins, he pleads for mercy, not on palliations of sin, but on God's well-known benevolence. <div eID="gen8702" type="x-p"/>
entries.083f832f108b1cb49c1d57aacedf6e7e7b01226a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5719"/><div sID="gen8703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5719"/><hi type="bold">8-9. upright--</hi>acting according to His promise.<div eID="gen8703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sinners--</hi>the general term, limited by the<div eID="gen8704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meek--</hi>who are penitent.<div eID="gen8705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the way--</hi>and his way--God's way of providence. <div eID="gen8706" type="x-p"/>
entries.69ab9817ba8845061b510e39a5969fb3cc56d9ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5721"/><div sID="gen8708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5721"/><hi type="bold">10. paths--</hi>similar sense--His modes of dealing (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.25.4">Psa 25:4</reference>).<div eID="gen8708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mercy and truth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.14.1-Job.14.22">Job 14:1-22</reference>), God's grace in promising and faithfulness in performing. <div eID="gen8709" type="x-p"/>
entries.b992699ed8e386213806c824ec46b0030859dc6c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5722"/><div sID="gen8710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5722"/>11. God's perfections of love, mercy, goodness, and truth are manifested (his name, compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Psa 9:10</reference>) in pardoning sin, and the greatness of sin renders pardon more needed. <div eID="gen8710" type="x-p"/>
entries.95d063aa51614b2bbb0cb6f3d6c0b49db92acaed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5723"/><div sID="gen8711" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5723"/>12-13. What he asks for himself is the common lot of all the pious. <div eID="gen8711" type="x-p"/>
entries.6785d2939e569ef38d2346f8ccfd47713958f4c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5725"/><div sID="gen8713" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5725"/><hi type="bold">14. The reason of the blessing explained--</hi>the pious enjoy communion with God (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.3.21">Pr 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.12">12</reference>), and, of course, learn His gracious terms of pardon. <div eID="gen8713" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d5182fe2bf537aaea2807136789cbfbdf408fb4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5726"/><div sID="gen8714" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5726"/>15. His trust in God is fixed.<div eID="gen8714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">net--</hi>is frequently used as a figure for dangers by enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.15">Psa 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.9">10:9</reference>). <div eID="gen8715" type="x-p"/>
entries.09774a41b0e091fd64e6f408f59bdd71dfa64fcd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5727"/><div sID="gen8716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5727"/>16-19. A series of earnest appeals for aid because God had seemed to desert him (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.13.1">Psa 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">17:13</reference>, &c.), his sins oppressed him, his enemies had enlarged his troubles and were multiplied, increasing in hate and violence (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.8">Psa 9:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.48">18:48</reference>). <div eID="gen8716" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce3463ae4be42fbc023d5987423a8a268d8ee324: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5728"/><div sID="gen8717" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5728"/><hi type="bold">20. keep my soul--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference>).<div eID="gen8717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put my trust--</hi>flee for refuge (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Psa 2:12</reference>). <div eID="gen8718" type="x-p"/>
entries.e54c99919d78385d59d425f6e73ad82522a4592a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5729"/><div sID="gen8719" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5729"/> <hi type="bold">21. In conscious innocence of the faults charged by his enemies, he confidently commits his cause to God. Some refer--</hi> <div eID="gen8719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8720" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">integrity, &c.--</hi>to God, meaning His covenant faithfulness. This sense, though good, is an unusual application of the terms. <div eID="gen8720" type="x-p"/>
entries.6fa54302c06e7897d39dd8a5b8bc2bc66ea59da3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5730"/><div sID="gen8721" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5730"/>22. Extend these blessings to all Thy people in all their distresses. <chapter eID="Ps.25"/>

entries.43eb508514e6e8c10ab24d985b03a73c8c395028: <div eID="gen19302" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19303" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19304" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19304" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19303" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19305" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, in great distress, calls upon God frequently, <reference osisRef="Psa.25.1-Psa.25.5">Psa 25:1-5</reference>; prays for pardon with the strong confidence of being heard, <reference osisRef="Psa.25.6-Psa.25.11">Psa 25:6-11</reference>; shows the blessedness of the righteous, <reference osisRef="Psa.25.12-Psa.25.14">Psa 25:12-14</reference>; again earnestly implores the Divine mercy; and prays for the restoration of Israel, <reference osisRef="Psa.25.15-Psa.25.22">Psa 25:15-22</reference>. <div eID="gen19305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19306" type="x-p"/> This Psalm seems to refer to the case of the captives in Babylon, who complain of oppression from their enemies, and earnestly beg the help and mercy of God. <div eID="gen19306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19307" type="x-p"/> It is the first of those called acrostic Psalms, i.e., Psalms each line of which begins with a several letter of the Hebrew alphabet in their common order. Of acrostic Psalms there are seven, viz., 25, 34, 37, <reference osisRef="Psa.111.1-Psa.111.10">Psa 111:1-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.112.1-Psa.112.10">Psa 112:1-10</reference>, 119, and 145. It is fashionable to be violent in encomiums on the Jews for the very faithful manner in which they have preserved the Hebrew Scriptures; but these encomiums are, in general, ill placed. Even this Psalm is a proof with what carelessness they have watched over the sacred deposit committed to their trust. The letter ו vau is wanting in the fifth verse, and ק koph in the eighteenth; the letter ר resh being twice inserted, once instead of ק koph, and a whole line added at the end, entirely out of the alphabetical series. <div eID="gen19307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19308" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19309" type="x-p"/> Do I lift up my soul - His soul was cast down, and by prayer and faith he endeavours to lift it up to God.
entries.965c3a0d4898a3aab0b77cdadd63ad45d5ec93d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19310" type="x-p"/> I trust in thee - I depend upon thy infinite goodness and mercy for my support and salvation. <div eID="gen19310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19311" type="x-p"/> Let me not be ashamed - Hide my iniquity, and forgive my guilt.
entries.35a93cf36df6506e4115bf834b6d714dbdafd163: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19312" type="x-p"/> Let none that wait on thee be ashamed - Though he had burden enough of his own, he felt for others in similar circumstances, and became an intercessor in their behalf. <div eID="gen19312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19313" type="x-p"/> Transgress without cause - Perhaps בוגדים bogedim may here mean idolatrous persons. "Let not them that wait upon and worship thee be ashamed: but they shall be ashamed who vainly worship, or trust in false gods." See <reference osisRef="Mal.2.11-Mal.2.16">Mal 2:11-16</reference>. The Chaldeans have evil entreated us, and oppressed us: they trust in their idols, let them see the vanity of their idolatry.
entries.2e8da043abb15f0857a72e03e66fbfe689a9b3b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19314" type="x-p"/> Show me thy ways - The psalmist wishes to know God's way, to be taught his path, and to be led into his truth. He cannot discern this way unless God show it; he cannot learn the path unless God teach it; and he cannot walk in God's truth unless God lead him: and even then, unless God continue to teach, he shall never fully learn the lessons of his salvation; therefore he adds, "Lead me in thy truth, and teach me;" <reference osisRef="Psa.25.5">Psa 25:5</reference>. <div eID="gen19314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19315" type="x-p"/> That he may get this showing, teaching, and leading, he comes to God, as the "God of his salvation;" and that he may not lose his labor, he "waits on him all the day." Many lose the benefit of their earnest prayers, because they do not persevere in them. They pray for a time; get remiss or discouraged; restrain prayer; and thus lose all that was already wrought for and in them.
entries.5ad7e2f95cbddede58039110ab7628f12b23c47c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19316" type="x-p"/> On thee do I wait - This is the line in which ו vau, the sixth letter in the order of the alphabet, is lost; for the line begins with א aleph, אותך othecha, "on thee." But four of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. have ואותך veothecha, "And upon thee." This restores the lost ו vau, which signifies "and." The Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, Arabic, Ethiopic, and Anglo-Saxon, preserve it.
entries.d430e91e2f0149687e3c25f210aeaab19c8c1d5f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19317" type="x-p"/> Remember, O Lord, thy tender mercies, and thy loving-kindness - The word רחמים rachamim, means the commiseration that a man feels in his bowels at the sight of distress. The second word, חסדים chasadim, signifies those kindnesses which are the offspring of a profusion of benevolence. <div eID="gen19317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19318" type="x-p"/> They have been ever of old - Thou wert ever wont to display thyself as a ceaseless fountain of good to all thy creatures.
entries.be9dde4c9ffe6323e3c643955ac5d0c0e5286357: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19319" type="x-p"/> Remember not the sins of my youth - Those which I have committed through inconsiderateness, and heat of passion. <div eID="gen19319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19320" type="x-p"/> According to thy mercy - As it is worthy of thy mercy to act according to the measure, the greatness, and general practice of thy mercy; so give me an abundant pardon, a plentiful salvation. <div eID="gen19320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19321" type="x-p"/> For thy goodness' sake - Goodness is the nature of God; mercy flows from that goodness.
entries.9b74e319a078edd10052ee743fdc721a4b575e68: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19322" type="x-p"/> Good and upright is the Lord - He is good in his nature, and righteous in his conduct. <div eID="gen19322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19323" type="x-p"/> Therefore will he teach sinners - Because he is good, he will teach sinners, though they deserve nothing but destruction: and because he is right, he will teach them the true way.
entries.ca8521eb5bd369d8ad130168cb93396de43809b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19324" type="x-p"/> The meek will he guide - ענוים anavim, the poor, the distressed; he will lead in judgment - he will direct them in their cause, and bring it to a happy issue, for he will show them the way in which they should go.
entries.563291e2550d8345700e76410d31c5277c915455: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19325" type="x-p"/> All the paths of the Lord - ארחות orchoth signifies the tracks or ruts made by the wheels of wagons by often passing over the same ground. Mercy and truth are the paths in which God constantly walks in reference to the children of men; and so frequently does he show them mercy, and so frequently does he fulfill his truth that his paths are earnestly discerned. How frequent, how deeply indented, and how multiplied are those tracks to every family and individual! Wherever we go, we see that God's mercy and truth have been there by the deep tracks they have left behind them. But he is more abundantly merciful to those who keep his covenant and his testimonies; i.e. those who are conformed, not only to the letter, but to the spirit of his pure religion.
entries.c559ded4ad0f4fe7fc07f81c5945b7010897036f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19326" type="x-p"/> For thy name's sake, O Lord, pardon - I have sinned; I need mercy; there is no reason why thou shouldst show it, but what thou drawest from the goodness of thy own nature.
entries.1df8bbcb5cf7ad0e030026153dfff2673c523962: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19327" type="x-p"/> That feareth the Lord - Who has a proper apprehension of his holiness, justice, and truth; and who, at the same time, sees himself a fallen spirit, and a transgressor of God's holy law, and consequently under the curse. That is the person that truly and reverently fears God. <div eID="gen19327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19328" type="x-p"/> Him shall he teach - Such a person has a teachable spirit. <div eID="gen19328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19329" type="x-p"/> The way that he shall choose - The way that in the course of Providence he has chosen, as the way in which he is to gain things honest in the sight of all men; God will bless him in it, and give him as much earthly prosperity as may be useful to his soul in his secular vocation.
entries.4f6308993c06734f4535dc714f6e164ad94c007e: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen19329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19330" type="x-p"/> His soul shall dwell at ease - בטוב תלין betob talin, "shall lodge in goodness;" this is the marginal reading in our version; and is preferable to that in the text. <div eID="gen19330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19331" type="x-p"/> His seed shall inherit - His posterity shall be blessed. For them many prayers have been sent up to God by their pious fathers; and God has registered these prayers in their behalf.
entries.708c62db4c4f9d3289b373f5bcf0f6526b555649: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen19331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19332" type="x-p"/> The secret of the Lord is with them - טוד sod, the secret assembly of the Lord is with them that fear him; many of them have a Church in their own house. <div eID="gen19332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19333" type="x-p"/> He will show them his covenant - He will let them see how great blessings he has provided for them that love him. Some refer this to the covenant of redemption by Christ Jesus.
entries.616d21ea79e51f97f2dc598af720092064d1d81f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen19333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19334" type="x-p"/> Mine eyes are ever toward the Lord - All my expectation is from him alone. If I get at any time entangled, he will pluck my feet out of the net.
entries.79efea8d3a8a3219fc074294631aed0eed1708f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen19334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19335" type="x-p"/> Turn thee unto me - Probably the prayer of the poor captives in Bablyon, which is continued through this and the remaining verses.
entries.f9ba04dbf5e717a50a17924deed29c6adecb805b: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen19335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19336" type="x-p"/> The troubles of may heart are enlarged - The evils of our captive state, instead of lessening, seem to multiply, and each to be extended.
entries.ced0ab299117753bd5227334e0f8c49f6f5cc8d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen19336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19337" type="x-p"/> Look upon mine affliction - See my distressed condition, and thy eye will affect thy heart. <div eID="gen19337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19338" type="x-p"/> Forgive all my sins - My sins are the cause of all my sufferings; forgive these. <div eID="gen19338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19339" type="x-p"/> This is the verse which should begin with the letter ק koph; but, instead of it, we have ר resh both here, where it should not be, and in the next verse where it should be. Dr. Kennicott reads קומה kumah, "arise," and Houbigant, קצר ketsar, "cut short." The word which began with ק koph has been long lost out of the verse, as every version seems to have read that which now stands in the Hebrew text.
entries.a40487e5f0f2f57c0f8d3459be265efcb242810e: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen19339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19340" type="x-p"/> Consider mine enemies - Look upon them, and thou wilt see how impossible it is that I should be able to resist and overcome them. They are many, they hate me, and their hatred drives them to acts of cruelty against me.
entries.0e17ff3c7f0d77986496a56f87de90b5b880749b: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen19340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19341" type="x-p"/> O keep my soul - Save me from sin, and keep me alive. <div eID="gen19341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19342" type="x-p"/> Let me not be ashamed - He ends as he began; see <reference osisRef="Psa.25.2">Psa 25:2</reference> : "Let me not be confounded, for I put my trust in thee."
entries.9f391d36284391439026717bc0517daca6c424fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen19342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19343" type="x-p"/> Let integrity and uprightness - I wish to have a perfect heart, and an upright life. This seems to be the meaning of these two words.
entries.f791e466e9bfef4457b28f0e673da6357ec0b363: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen19343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19344" type="x-p"/> Redeems Israel, O God - The people are prayed for in the preceding verses as if one person; now he includes the whole, lest his own personal necessities should narrow his heart. and cause him to forget his fellow sufferers. <div eID="gen19344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19345" type="x-p"/> This verse stands out of the order of the Psalm; and does not appear to have formed a part of the alphabetical arrangement. It is a general prayer for the redemption of Israel from captivity; and may well be applied to those of the true Israel who are seeking for complete redemption from the power, the guilt, and the pollution of sin; and from all the troubles that spring from it. And let it be ever known, that God alone can redeem Israel.  <chapter eID="Ps.25"/> <div eID="gen19345" type="x-p"/>

entries.2f0bcddc6d8514c1742c6760ba8169997615fcdd: <div eID="gen9301" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Prayer for Gracious Protection and Guidance</title> <div sID="gen9302" type="x-p"/> A question similar to the question, <hi type="italic">Who may ascend the mountain of Jahve</hi>? which <reference osisRef="Ps.24.1-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:1-10</reference> propounded, is thrown out by Ps 25, <, <hi type="italic">Who is he that feareth Jahve</hi>? in order to answer it in great and glorious promises. It is calmly confident prayer for help against one’s foes, and for God’s instructing, pardoning, and leading grace. It is without any definite background indicating the history of the times in which it was composed; and also without any clearly marked traits of individuality. But it is one of the nine alphabetical Psalms of the whole collection, and the companion to Ps 34, to which it corresponds even in many peculiarities of the acrostic structure. For both Psalms have no ו strophe; they are parallel both as to sound and meaning in the beginnings of the מ, ע, and the first פ strophes; and both Psalms, after having gone through the alphabet, have a פ strophe added as the concluding one, whose beginning and contents are closely related. This homogeneousness points to one common author. We see nothing in the alphabetical arrangement at least, which even here as in <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Ps 9-10</reference> is handled very freely and not fully carried out, to hinder us from regarding David as this author. But, in connection with the general ethical and religious character of the Psalm, it is wanting in positive proofs of this. In its universal character and harmony with the plan of redemption Ps 25 coincides with many post-exilic Psalms. It contains nothing but what is common to the believing consciousness of the church in every age; nothing specifically belonging to the Old Testament and Israelitish, hence Theodoret says: ἁρμόζει μάλιστα τοῖς ἐξ ἐθνῶν κεκλημένοις. The introits for the second and third Quadragesima Sundays are taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.25.6">Psa 25:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">Psa 25:15</reference>; hence these Sundays are called <hi type="italic">Reminiscere</hi> and <hi type="italic">Oculi</hi>. Paul Gerhardt’s hymn <hi type="italic">“Nach dir, o Herr, verlanget mich”</hi> is a beautiful poetical rendering of this Psalm.
entries.979e73c0d248b909db32e7e5817cd57fa6753882: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.1-Ps.25.2">Psa 25:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9303" type="x-p"/> The Psalm begins, like <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11">Psa 16:1-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.23.1">Psa 23:1</reference>, with a monostich. <reference osisRef="Ps.25.2">Psa 25:2</reference> is the ב strophe, אלהי (unless one is disposed to read בך אלהי according to the position of the words in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2">Psa 31:2</reference>), after the manner of the interjections in the tragedians, e.g., oo'moi, not being reckoned as belonging to the verse (J. D. Köhler). In need of help and full of longing for deliverance he raises his soul, drawn away from earthly desires, to Jahve (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.4">Psa 86:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">Psa 143:8</reference>), the God who alone can grant him that which shall truly satisfy his need. His ego, which has the soul within itself, directs his soul upwards to Him whom he calls אלהי, because in believing confidence he clings to Him and is united with Him. The two אל declare what Jahve is not to allow him to experience, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2">Psa 31:2</reference>, Psa 31:18. According to <reference osisRef="Ps.25.19">Psa 25:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.20">Psa 25:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.17">Psa 38:17</reference>, it is safer to construe לי with יעלצוּ (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.71.10">Psa 71:10</reference>), as also in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">Psa 27:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.30.2">Psa 30:2</reference>, Mic 7:8, although it would be possible to construe it with אויבי (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.144.2">Psa 144:2</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Ps.25.3">Psa 25:3</reference> the confident expectation of the individual is generalised.
entries.bf81539f1171c2846cb4f3c23b87a6ef8eef32c8: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.3">Psa 25:3</reference> <div eID="gen9303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9304" type="x-p"/> That wherewith the praying one comforts himself is no peculiar personal prerogative, but the certain, joyous prospect of all believers: ἡ ἐλπίς ου ̓ καταισχύνει, Rom 5:5. These are called קויך (קוה participle to קוּה ot elp, just as דּבר is the participle to דּבּר). Hope is the eye of faith which looks forth clear and fixedly into the future. With those who hope in Jahve, who do not allow themselves to be in any way disconcerted respecting Him, are contrasted those who act treacherously towards Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.158">Psa 119:158</reference>, Aq., Symm., Theodot. οἱ ἀποστατοῦντες), and that ריקם, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi> - and it can only mean this-from vain and worthless pretexts, and therefore from wanton unconscientiousness.
entries.993c5755bf77a88b6acf682c026959097115e2ec: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.4">Psa 25:4</reference> <div eID="gen9304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9305" type="x-p"/> Recognising the infamy of such black ingratitude, he prays for instruction as to the ways which he must take according to the precepts of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.22">Psa 18:22</reference>). The will of God, it is true, lies before us in God’s written word, but the expounder required for the right understanding of that word is God Himself. He prays Him for knowledge; but in order to make what he knows a perfect and living reality, he still further needs the grace of God, viz., both His enlightening and also His guiding grace.
entries.3f4a5880fcfc5eed050a9d8bb5be4f03d9ac6053: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.5">Psa 25:5</reference> <div eID="gen9305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9306" type="x-p"/> His truth is the lasting and self-verifying fact of His revelation of grace. To penetrate into this truth and to walk in it (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.3">Psa 26:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.11">Psa 86:11</reference>) without God, is a contradiction in its very self. Therefore the psalmist prays, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.35">Psa 119:35</reference>, οδήγησόν με ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ σου (lxx <hi type="italic">Cod. Alex.</hi>; whereas <hi type="italic">Cod. Vat</hi>. ἐπὶ τὴν..., cf. Joh 16:13). He prays thus, for his salvation comes from Jahve, yea Jahve is his salvation. He does not hope for this or that, but for Him, all the day, i.e., unceasingly,<note placement="foot">Hupfeld thinks the accentuation inappropriate; the first half of the verse, however, really extends to ישׁעי, and consists of two parts, of which the second is the confirmation of the first: the second half contains a relatively new thought. The sequence of the accents: <hi type="italic">Rebia magnum, Athnach</hi>, therefore fully accords with the matter.</note> for everything worth hoping for, everything that can satisfy the longing of the soul, is shut up in Him. All mercy or grace, however, which proceeds from Him, has its foundation in His compassion and condescension.
entries.3e00ab4740f2b7918de3dbb1d844e69f62cfea3b: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.6">Psa 25:6</reference> <div eID="gen9306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9307" type="x-p"/> The supplicatory <hi type="italic">reminiscere</hi> means, may God never forget to exercise His pity and grace towards him, which are (as the plurals imply) so rich and superabundant. The ground on which the prayer is based is introduced with כּי (<hi type="italic">nam</hi>, or even <hi type="italic">quoniam</hi>). God’s compassion and grace are as old in their operation and efficacy as man’s feebleness and sin; in their counsels they are eternal, and therefore have also in themselves the pledge of eternal duration (<reference osisRef="Ps.100.5">Psa 100:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.17">Psa 103:17</reference>).
entries.6c5e8c1a5fdedab36e1e6a216cb0a60e27e654f1: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.7">Psa 25:7</reference> <div eID="gen9307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9308" type="x-p"/> May Jahve not remember the faults of his youth (חטּאות), into which lust and thoughtlessness have precipitated him, nor the transgressions (פּשׁעים), by which even in maturer and more thoughtful years he has turned the grace of God into licentiousness and broken off his fellowship with Him (פּשׁע בּ, of defection); but may He, on the contrary, turn His remembrance to him (זכר ל as in <reference osisRef="Ps.136.23">Psa 136:23</reference>) in accordance with His grace or loving-kindness, which אתּה challenges as being the form of self-attestation most closely corresponding to the nature of God. <hi type="italic">Memor esto quidem mei, observes Augustine, non secundum iram, qua ego dignus sum, sed secundum misericordiam tuam, quae te digna est.</hi> For God is טּוב, which is really equivalent to saying, He is ἀγάπη. The next distich shows that טוּב is intended here of God’s goodness, and not, as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Neh.9.35">Neh 9:35</reference>, of His abundance of possessions.
entries.4799bdb96a871eda5389c277e26c808f399b40c5: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.8">Psa 25:8</reference> <div eID="gen9308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9309" type="x-p"/> The בּ with הורה denotes the way, i.e., the right way (<reference osisRef="Job.31.7">Job 31:7</reference>), as the sphere and subject of the instruction, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Psa 32:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.11">Pro 4:11</reference>; Job 27:11. God condescends to sinners in order to teach them the way that leads to life, for He is טוב־וישׂר; well-doing is His delight, and, if His anger be not provoked (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.18.27">Psa 18:27</reference></hi>), He has only the sincerest good intention in what He does.
entries.ed7ec0850544e71e1d0f2ed6ac5e88c05a82297b: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.9">Psa 25:9</reference> <div eID="gen9309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9310" type="x-p"/> The shortened form of the future stands here, according to Ges. §128, 2, rem., instead of the full form (which, viz., ידרך, is perhaps meant); for the connection which treats of general facts, does not admit of its being taken as optative. The ב (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.25.5">Psa 25:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.7">Psa 107:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.35">Psa 119:35</reference>) denotes the sphere of the guidance. משׁפּט is the right so far as it is traversed, i.e., practised or carried out. In this course of right He leads the ענוים, and teaches them the way that is pleasing to Himself. ענוים is the one word for the gentle, <hi type="italic">mansueti</hi>, and the humble, <hi type="italic">modesti</hi>. Jerome uses these words alternately in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.25.9">Psa 25:9</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.25.9">Psa 25:9</reference></hi>; but the poet designedly repeats the one word - the cardinal virtue of ענוה -  here with the preponderating notion of lowliness. Upon the self-righteous and self-sufficient He would be obliged to force Himself even against their will. He wants disciples eager to learn; and how richly He rewards those who guard what they have learnt!
entries.e5d315171923f6b1d415324b964bff7464c0d25c: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.10">Psa 25:10</reference> <div eID="gen9310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9311" type="x-p"/> The paths intended, are those which He takes with men in accordance with His revealed will and counsel. These paths are חסד loving-kindness, mercy, or grace, for the salvation of men is their goal, and אמת truth, for they give proof at every step of the certainty of His promises. But only they who keep His covenant and His testimonies faithfully and obediently shall share in this mercy and truth. To the psalmist the name of Jahve, which unfolds itself in mercy and truth, is precious. Upon it he bases the prayer that follows.
entries.3e9390f4b27e7a9f3ab907eb3c39160e8faa4879: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.11">Psa 25:11</reference> <div eID="gen9311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9312" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">perf. consec.</hi> is attached to the יהי, which is, according to the sense, implied in למען שׁמך, just as in other instances it follows adverbial members of a clause, placed first for the sake of emphasis, when those members have reference to the future, Ges. §126, rem. 1. Separate and manifold sins (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.7">Psa 25:7</reference>) are all comprehended in עון, which is in other instances also the collective word for the corruption and the guilt of sin. כּי gives the ground of the need and urgency of the petition. A great and multiform load of sin lies upon him, but the name of God, i.e., His nature that has become manifest in His mercy and truth, permits him to ask and to hope for forgiveness, not for the sake of anything whatever that he has done, but just for the sake of this name (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.7">Jer 14:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Isa 43:25</reference>). How happy therefore is he who fears God, in this matter!
entries.4933934d4f6829e2b949b50f4a915f8f43f99e54: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.12">Psa 25:12</reference> <div eID="gen9312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9313" type="x-p"/> The question: <hi type="italic">quisnam est vir</hi>, which resembles <reference osisRef="Ps.34.13">Psa 34:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.43">Psa 107:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.10">Isa 50:10</reference>, is only propounded in order to draw attention to the person who bears the character described, and then to state what such an one has to expect. In prose we should have a relative antecedent clause instead, viz., <hi type="italic">qui </hi>(<hi type="italic">quisquis</hi>)<hi type="italic">talis est qui Dominum vereatur</hi>.<note placement="foot">The verb <hi type="italic">ver-eri</hi>, which signifies “to guard one’s self, defend one’s self from anything” according to its radical notion, has nothing to do with ירא (ורא).</note> <div eID="gen9313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9314" type="x-p"/> The attributive יבהר, (<hi type="italic">viam</hi>)<hi type="italic">quam eligat</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.48.17">Isa 48:17</reference>), might also be referred to God: in which He takes delight (lxx); but parallels like <reference osisRef="Ps.119.30">Psa 119:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.173">Psa 119:173</reference>, favour the rendering: which he should choose. Among all the blessings which fall to the lot of him who fears God, the first place is given to this, that God raises him above the vacillation and hesitancy of human opinion.
entries.52e1a35f3416fd1d8ec02c3f6d870a39521f595a: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.13">Psa 25:13</reference> <div eID="gen9314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9315" type="x-p"/> The verb לין (לוּן), probably equivalent to ליל (from ליל) signifies to tarry the night, to lodge. Good, i.e., inward and outward prosperity, is like the place where such an one turns in and finds shelter and protection. And in his posterity will be fulfilled what was promised to the patriarchs and to the people delivered from Egypt, viz., possession of the land, or as this promise runs in the New Testament, of the earth, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.5">Mat 5:5</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.37.11">Psa 37:11</reference>), Rev 5:10.
entries.82dd83741417e78a6dbdded793930ef7f819815e: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference> <div eID="gen9315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9316" type="x-p"/> The lxx renders סוד, κραταίωμα, as though it were equivalent to יסוד. The reciprocal נוסד, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.2">Psa 2:2</reference> (which see), leads one to the right primary signification. Starting from the primary meaning of the root סד, “to be or to make tight, firm, compressed,” סוד signifies a being closely pressed together for the purpose of secret communication and converse, confidential communion or being together, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.8">Psa 89:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1">Psa 111:1</reference> (Symm. ὁμιλία), then the confidential communication itself, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.15">Psa 55:15</reference>, a secret (Aquila ἀπόῤῥητον, Theod. μυστήριον). So here: He opens his mind without any reserve, speaks confidentially with those who fear Him; cf. the derivative passage <reference osisRef="Prov.3.32">Pro 3:32</reference>, and an example of the thing itself in Gen 18:17. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Psa 25:14</reference></hi> the infinitive with ל, according to Ges. §132, rem. 1, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.38.20">Isa 38:20</reference>, is an expression for the <hi type="italic">fut. periphrast.: faedus suum notum facturus est iis</hi>; the position of the words is like <reference osisRef="Dan.2.16">Dan 2:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.18">Dan 2:18</reference>; Dan 4:15. הודיע is used of the imparting of not merely intellectual, but experimental knowledge. Hitzig renders it differently, viz., to enlighten them. But the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. is not intended to be used thus absolutely even in 2Sa 7:21. בּריתו is the object; it is intended of the rich and deep and glorious character of the covenant revelation. The poet has now on all sides confirmed the truth, that every good gift comes down from above, from the God of salvation; and he returns to the thought from which he started.
entries.1cc572b247d5e5f683ee5e7d724b83f7c9e2198b: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">Psa 25:15</reference> <div eID="gen9316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9317" type="x-p"/> He who keeps his eyes constantly directed towards God (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.8">Psa 141:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.123.1">Psa 123:1</reference>), is continually in a praying mood, which cannot remain unanswered. תּמיד corresponds to ἀδιαλείπτως in 1Th 5:17. The aim of this constant looking upwards to God, in this instance, is deliverance out of the enemy’s net. He can and will pull him out (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.5">Psa 31:5</reference>) of the net of complicated circumstances into which he has been ensnared without any fault of his own.
entries.781f521ac8615d060d625be1b21ec1ab679af615: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.16">Psa 25:16</reference> <div eID="gen9317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9318" type="x-p"/> The rendering “regard me,” so far as פּנה אל means God’s observant and sympathising turning to any one (lxx ἐπιβλέπειν), corresponds to <reference osisRef="Ps.86.16">Psa 86:16</reference>; Lev 26:9. For this he longs, for men treat him as a stranger and refuse to have anything to do with him. יחיד is the only one of his kind, one who has no companion, therefore the isolated one. The recurrence of the same sounds עני אני is designedly not avoided. To whom could he, the isolated one, pour forth his affliction, to whom could he unveil his inmost thoughts and feelings? to God alone! To Him he can bring all his complaints, to Him he can also again and again always make supplication.
entries.b5fd06fca4e40f0740b51ea0d5dd754d624d9f91: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.17">Psa 25:17</reference> <div eID="gen9318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9319" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הרחיב signifies to make broad, and as a transitive denominative applied to the mind and heart: to make a broad space = to expand one’s self (cf. as to the idea, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.13">Lam 2:13</reference>, “great as the sea is thy misfortune”), lxx ἐπληθύνθησαν, perhaps originally it was ἐπλατηύνθησαν. Accordingly הרחיבוּ is admissible so far as language is concerned; but since it gives only a poor antithesis to צרות it is to be suspected. The original text undoubtedly was הרחיב וממצוקותי (הרחיב, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.77.2">Psa 77:2</reference>, or הרחיב, as e.g., in 2Ki 8:6): the straits of my heart do Thou enlarge (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.119.32">Psa 119:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.11">2Co 6:11</reference>) and bring me out of my distresses (Hitzig and others).
entries.028c53d682032d9c9cecf61963b9ce4c64ea8c88: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.18-Ps.25.19">Psa 25:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen9319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9320" type="x-p"/> The falling away of the ק is made up for by a double ר strophe. Even the lxx has ἴδε twice over. The seeing that is prayed for, is in both instances a seeing into his condition, with which is conjoined the notion of interposing on his behalf, though the way and manner thereof is left to God. נשׂא ל, with the object in the dative instead of the accusative (<hi type="italic">tollere peccata</hi>), signifies to bestow a taking away, i.e., forgiveness, upon any one (synon. סלח ל). It is pleasing to the New Testament consciousness that God’s vengeance is not expressly invoked upon his enemies. כּי is an expansive <hi type="italic">quod</hi> as in Gen 1:4. שׂנאת חמס with an attributive genitive is hatred, which springs from injustice and ends in injustice.
entries.dd10d7a4964a9a0aafc36897eff7e9517c8a0cd2: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.20">Psa 25:20</reference> <div eID="gen9320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9321" type="x-p"/> He entreats for preservation and deliverance from God; and that He may not permit his hope to be disappointed (אל־אבושׁ, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.13">1Ch 21:13</reference>, instead of אל־אבושׁה which is usual in other instances). This his hope rests indeed in Him: he has taken refuge in Him and therefore He cannot forsake him, He cannot let him be destroyed.
entries.dc4498d77a503a802883f3f091a6fd2fb4e65505: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.21">Psa 25:21</reference> <div eID="gen9321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9322" type="x-p"/> Devoutness that fills the whole man, that is not merely half-hearted and hypocritical, is called תּם; and uprightness that follows the will of God without any bypaths and forbidden ways is called ישׁר. These two radical virtues (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.1.1">Job 1:1</reference>) he desires to have as his guardians on his way which is perilous not only by reason of outward foes, but also on account of his own sinfulness. These custodians are not to let him pass out of their sight, lest he should be taken away from them (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">Psa 40:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.28">Pro 20:28</reference>). He can claim this for himself, for the cynosure of his hope is God, from whom proceed תם and ישׁר like good angels.
entries.67798e97b5908ae72a7e73d1b1975d0716c3cdb3: <reference osisRef="Ps.25.22">Psa 25:22</reference> <div eID="gen9322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9323" type="x-p"/> His experience is not singular, but the enmity of the world and sin bring all who belong to the people of God into straits just as they have him. And the need of the individual will not cease until the need of the whole undergoes a radical remedy. Hence the intercessory prayer of this meagre closing distich, whose connection with what precedes is not in this instance so close as in Ps 34:23. It looks as though it was only added when Ps 25 came to be used in public worship; and the change of the name of God favours this view. Both Psalms close with a פ in excess of the alphabet. Perhaps the first פ represents the π, and the second the φ; for <reference osisRef="Ps.25.16">Psa 25:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.17">Psa 34:17</reference> follow words ending in a consonant, and <reference osisRef="Ps.25.22">Psa 25:22</reference>; 34:23, words ending in a vowel. Or is it a propensity for giving a special representation of the final letters, just as these are sometimes represented, though not always perfectly, at the close of the hymns of the synagogue (<hi type="italic">pijutim</hi>)?  <chapter eID="Ps.25"/> <div eID="gen9323" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 25.
This psalm consists of meditations mingled with prayers. Being rudely treated, and grievously distressed, by the cruelty of his enemies, David, in order to obtain assistance from God, first acknowledges that God had justly made use of this as a means of chastising and punishing him for his sins; and, therefore, he prays for their forgiveness, that he may at once enjoy assurance of the divine favor, and obtain deliverance. He then implores the aid of the Holy Spirit, that, sustained by it, he might, even in the midst of so many temptations, continue in the fear of God. And in various places he intermingles meditation, as the means of stirring up himself to increased confidence in God, and of withdrawing his thoughts from the allurements of the world.
A Psalm of David.
Psalm 25:1-3
1. Unto thee, O Jehovah! I have lifted up my soul 2. O my God! I have put my trust in thee; let me not be ashamed; let not mine enemies rejoice over me. 3. Yea, none of those that wait on thee shall be ashamed; but they shall be ashamed that deal falsely without cause.
 
1. Unto thee, O Jehovah! etc The Psalmist declares at the very outset, that he is not driven hither and thither, after the manner of the ungodly, but that he directs all his desires and prayers to God alone. Nothing is more inconsistent with true and sincere prayer to God, than to waver and gaze about as the heathen do, for some help from the world; and at the same time to forsake God, or not to betake ourselves directly to his guardianship and protection. Those who imagine that David here declares that he had devoted himself entirely to God, as if he had offered up himself in sacrifice, do not properly understand the import of the passage. The meaning rather is, that in order to strengthen the hope of obtaining his request, he declares, what is of the greatest importance in prayer, that he had his hope fixed in God, and that he was not ensnared by the allurements of the world, or prevented from lifting up his soul fully and unfeignedly to God. In order, therefore, that we may pray aright to God, let us be directed by this rule — not to distract our minds by various and uncertain hopes, nor to depend on worldly aid, but to yield to God the honor of lifting up our hearts to him in sincere and earnest prayer. Moreover, although the verb is properly rendered, I will lift up, yet I have followed other interpreters in changing it into the past tense, I have lifted up By the future tense, however, David denotes a continued act.
